title: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Flexor Digitorum Superficialis Muscle -- Introduction
content: The flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS), formerly known as the flexor digitorum sublimis, is the largest of the extrinsic flexors of the forearm (see Image. Flexor Digitorum Superficialis). It forms the intermediate muscle layer between the superficial and deep muscle groups of the forearm. [1] It contains 4 digital components, each with a tendon that inserts into the corresponding finger. The flexor digitorum superficialis is the primary flexor of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints of the middle phalanges, but it also assists in flexion of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints.

title: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Flexor Digitorum Superficialis Muscle -- Structure and Function
content: The flexor digitorum superficialis muscle has 2 origins. The humeroulnar head originates from the medial epicondyle of the humerus and the coronoid process of the ulna. The radial head originates on the upper half of the volar aspect of the radial shaft. The median nerve and ulnar artery enter the forearm by passing between the humeroulnar and radial heads of the flexor digitorum superficialis muscle. title: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Flexor Digitorum Superficialis Muscle -- Structure and Function
content: The flexor digitorum superficialis flexes the middle phalanges of the medial 4 digits at the proximal interphalangeal joints. It also flexes the proximal phalanges at the metacarpophalangeal joints and the wrist joint. Flexor digitorum superficialis can flex each finger it serves independently. [1] The flexor digitorum superficialis is 1 of the long flexors of the digits, along with the flexor digitorum profundus. The flexor digitorum profundus flexes the digits slowly. Flexor digitorum superficialis reinforces this action when speed and flexion are required against resistance.

title: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Flexor Digitorum Superficialis Muscle -- Embryology
content: In the 4th week of development, the small upper limb buds form. [1] The limb bud is an outgrowth of somatic mesoderm, forming muscles, nerves, and vasculature, as well as lateral plate mesoderm, which forms bone, cartilage, and tendon into the ectoderm. [3] By week 7, every upper limb muscle can be grossly identified and contains muscle fibers. The more superficial muscles, such as the flexor digitorum superficialis, differentiate before the deeper muscles.

title: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Flexor Digitorum Superficialis Muscle -- Blood Supply and Lymphatics
content: The primary blood supply to the flexor digitorum superficialis muscle is from the ulnar artery. Lymphatic drainage of the upper limb occurs via the axillary lymph nodes.

title: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Flexor Digitorum Superficialis Muscle -- Physiologic Variants
content: Type I: A small muscle attached to the flexor digitorum superficialis tendon proximally and the index finger distally. During digital flexion, this muscle invades the carpal tunnel and could cause intermittent symptoms related to median nerve compression.

title: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Flexor Digitorum Superficialis Muscle -- Surgical Considerations
content: Flexor digitorum superficialis tenodesis, also known as the superficialis sling, is an operation that is used to treat swan neck deformity, a condition characterized by hypertension of the PIP joint of the finger and flexion posture of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint. [11] The goal of the procedure is to create a static volar restraint against hyperextension. The flexor digitorum superficialis muscle is often used in tendon transfer surgeries. There is a wide range of approaches, but the surgeon must have adequate access to both the point of incision, where the FDS slips off, and the point where the tendon is secured. The main approaches include funneling the tendon through the proximal phalanx, connecting it to the A1 or A2 pulley, or securing it to the proximal phalanx with bone anchors. [11] Following the operation, the affected PIP joint should be immobilized in extension for about 6 weeks with a splint. One complication that can arise with this procedure is the formation of a flexion contracture exceeding the desired degree. However, there is no consensus in the literature on the optimal angle of PIP joint flexion during tenodesis. [11]

title: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Flexor Digitorum Superficialis Muscle -- Surgical Considerations
content: The carpal tunnel release (CTR) procedure is an option when patients who are suffering from carpal tunnel syndrome do not respond to all non-operative therapies. [12] The 2 main approaches, open and endoscopic, both have well-characterized risks and benefits documented in the literature. Regardless of etiology, open CTR (OCTR) is the current gold standard for treating this condition and involves decompressing the median nerve by dividing the transverse carpal ligament (TCL). [13] Endoscopic CTR (ECTR) is a single-port surgical technique that also involves transection of the TCL but carries at least an increased theoretical risk of transection or injury to any of the carpal tunnel constituents. [13] Relief of CTS symptoms and full finger range of motion are usually achieved in uncomplicated cases at the 2-week postoperative stage, and most individuals can return to full activity after 6 weeks.

title: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Flexor Digitorum Superficialis Muscle -- Clinical Significance
content: Modified Baker's test: Ask the patient to flex the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint of the little finger alone while the other fingers are held extended by the examiner. The little and ring fingers are then released to flex together to observe the proximal interphalangeal joint flexion improvement. Suppose the patient cannot flex the proximal interphalangeal joint of the little finger while other fingers are restrained in extension. In that case, however, the patient can flex the proximal interphalangeal joint of the 5th digit while the 4th digit is released, indicating the absence of the 5th tendon of flexor digitorum superficialis. Bilateral palms test: Ask the patient to place their bilateral palms and corresponding fingers face to face, with the hands resting on the patient's own fingers. While the little finger is ordered to flex, the adjacent fingers' influence can be observed, apparently if there is a connection between the little finger and the adjacent fingers. [14]

title: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Flexor Digitorum Superficialis Muscle -- Clinical Significance
content: Swan neck deformity is the hyperextension of the PIP joint with flexion of the DIP joint, most commonly occurring secondary to rheumatoid arthritis, cerebral palsy, connective tissue disorders such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, or trauma. [15] [16] This deformity can make it difficult to flex the middle interphalangeal joint because tendons are located in this region. As a result, a snapping sensation can occur during flexion. Over time, swan neck deformities can become stiff and lead to long-term disability. [15] Treatment of the swan neck deformity is largely dependent on severity but can include splinting or surgical intervention of the affected finger.

title: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Flexor Digitorum Superficialis Muscle -- Clinical Significance
content: Carpal tunnel syndrome is the most common peripheral nerve entrapment syndrome. This condition can occur secondary to a retracted flexor digitorum superficialis tendon that invades the tunnel. Patients with CTS often present with intermittent numbness in their thumb, index, and middle fingers. Patients may also complain of discomfort in their wrist and palm of the affected hand that worsens throughout the night, weakness, and loss of grip strength. A common physical exam finding is a positive Phalen test, a sensitive and specific test for CTS that is usually present in moderate-to-severe cases. [17] The patient would be asked to flex their wrists and hold the dorsal aspects of their hands together for 1 minute. A positive test is determined by the presence of tingling in the thumb, index, and middle fingers, as well as the side of the medial half of the ring finger. Carpal tunnel syndrome can be managed surgically with a carpal tunnel release or non-operatively with an ultrasound-guided steroid injection or wrist splint. [12] Early surgery is typically an option with clinical evidence of median nerve denervation or when the patient elects surgery as their preferred option.
